title: Naso: lift up the heads (Numbers 4:22)
hook: the census phrase means both "count" and "lift up"

segments.voice: Yesterday the holy things were wrapped in blue for the road, and your line was cover what's holy. Did something precious get a layer of care? Today, a new portion. Day four hundred thirty-six.

In prison, in Genesis, Joseph listens to two men's dreams. To the royal cupbearer he says: in three days Pharaoh will lift up your head, and give you back your job. To the royal baker he says: in three days Pharaoh will lift up your head, too. Then he finishes the sentence. Off you. The same Hebrew phrase, lift up the head, means a pardon for one man and a hanging for the other. Hold on to that phrase. It comes back in this week's portion, and it isn't about dreams. It's about counting.
screen: `TWO DREAMS IN PRISON.` → `LIFT UP YOUR HEAD.` → `A PARDON, OR A HANGING.`

segments.voice: The new portion is called Naso, from its first instruction. God tells Moses to take the sum of the sons of Gershon. In Hebrew: naso et rosh, literally, lift up the head. That's the Bible's ordinary phrase for taking a census. You don't count heads; you lift them. Commentators have long noticed the double edge, the one Joseph's dreams show. Being counted can raise you up, or it can single you out. Some read the census itself as a choice about which it will be. To count someone by name, standing before Moses, is to lift them: you matter, you're on the list, you belong. Then look at who's being counted. Gershon was Levi's eldest son. Yet in the order of service, Kohath, the younger clan, was counted first, because Kohath carried the ark. Gershon's clan carried the curtains, the coverings, the hangings and the ropes. Soft goods. Not glamorous. And the verse adds two small Hebrew words: gam hem, them also. Take the sum of the sons of Gershon too. Some commentators read those words as a deliberate lift for the clan that might have felt second. They count. Their load counts. The same root, nun, sin, alef, lift or carry, runs all through this portion. It's the word for carrying the sanctuary on your shoulders. It'll come back soon, in a blessing, when God lifts up a face. In Naso, to count is to carry, and to carry is to lift.
screen: `NASO ET ROSH: LIFT THE HEAD.` · `COUNTED: RAISED, OR SINGLED OUT.` · `GERSHON: THE SOFT LOADS.` · `GAM HEM: THEM ALSO.` · then, large: `COUNTING IS LIFTING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: lift one person's spirit. Breathe, and think of the Gershonites in your world: the people who carry the soft loads. The one who handles the paperwork, does the laundry, sends the reminders, keeps the group chat from falling apart. The second child, the backup singer, the assistant coach. Pick one whose head could use lifting. Think of exactly what you'd say: not thanks for everything, but thanks for this, specifically. The bell holds the time.
Naso. Lift up: the first word of this week's portion, the Bible's way of saying count, and its way of saying you matter.
Your line: counting is lifting. Today, say the specific thank-you you planned, to someone whose work usually goes uncounted. Day four hundred thirty-six.

howItsDone: Naso is the longest weekly portion of the Torah, read in late spring, usually just after Shavuot. Its opening phrase, naso et rosh, is studied as a lesson in how being counted can lift a person up.

myth: the Hebrew for taking a census is lift up the head
naso et rosh: to count is, literally, to lift.
Kohath carried the ark; Gershon carried the curtains and coverings.
in Joseph's prison, lift up your head always meant good news
for the baker, it meant his head lifted off him.

fork.setup: Kohath, the younger clan, carries the ark and is counted first. Gershon, the eldest, carries curtains. how does the verse count Gershon?
options: it skips them; their work is minor.
it adds "them also": lift up their heads too.
it counts them with the other tribes.
fork.reveal: naso et rosh bnei Gershon gam hem: lift up the heads of Gershon's sons too. some commentators hear a deliberate lift.

original.note: Hebrew: lift up the head. the Bible's phrase for taking a census.

trapdoor: what you thought: naso means count.
what it means: it means lift; to take a census is to lift up heads.
what a scholar hears: the same phrase, naso et rosh, means restoration for the cupbearer and execution for the baker in Genesis 40.

notes: The reading of 'gam hem' as a lift for Gershon (counted after the younger Kohath) is found in several commentators (e.g. Or HaChaim, among others); please name a specific source or soften to 'some commentators'.
'Naso is the longest weekly portion' (176 verses) is widely stated; confirm.
The nun-sin-alef root is said to return 'in a blessing' (Numbers 6:26, yisa); a gentle forward reference, not taught today.
